title: Policy unpredictability biggest deterrent to foreign capital: US Envoy | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:17
-     - 205

US Ambassador Eric Meyer - Pic by Upul Abayasekara

By Charumini de Silva

US Ambassador Eric Meyer yesterday identified policy and regulatory unpredictability as the single greatest deterrent to foreign investment in Sri Lanka, urging the country to strengthen transparency, intellectual property (IP) protection and fair competition to unlock greater bilateral business opportunities.

Addressing the 10th Annual General Meeting of the Sri Lanka–USA Business Council (SLUSABC) Meyer said sudden policy shifts and project reversals made it difficult for foreign investors to commit capital to long-term ventures, despite the progress Sri Lanka had achieved.

“Sri Lanka has indeed made significant progress, but policy and regulatory unpredictability remain the single greatest deterrent to foreign capital,” he said.

The Ambassador said sustainable economic growth required a predictable business environment, backed by strong intellectual property rights and transparent regulation, adding that these factors were critical to investment decisions by American companies.

Meyer, who said he had recently begun his assignment in Sri Lanka, reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to expanding bilateral economic and commercial ties and pledged to work with the private sector to address barriers to investment.

The US Embassy had recently secured funding to bring American technical expertise to support the modernisation of Sri Lanka’s ports, energy and high-tech sectors, he said.

“Our commitment extends beyond commercial trade,” Meyer said, highlighting the potential for technical cooperation alongside greater commercial engagement.

He noted that US companies offered expertise and innovation across technology, energy, infrastructure and logistics, creating opportunities for deeper collaboration between the two countries.

Meyer also encouraged Sri Lankan businesses to explore expansion opportunities in the United States, including participation in the upcoming ‘SelectUSA Investment Summit’, underscoring the importance of developing a two-way investment relationship rather than focusing solely on attracting American capital to Sri Lanka.

The Ambassador commended the Business Council for its work over the past year in promoting improvements to Sri Lanka’s regulatory framework and business environment, strengthening bilateral economic relations and raising awareness of the importance of IP protection in attracting US investment.

He said these efforts addressed issues that American businesses considered when assessing investment destinations.

“The United States remains fully committed to expanding the economic and commercial ties between our two nations,” Meyer said, adding that strengthening these links would be a priority during his tenure.

He called on the Council’s business leaders to use their influence to advance reforms, arguing that the private sector could play a significant role in translating policy discussions into tangible changes.

“As market leaders, you have the credibility to push for these reforms. The conversations you’ve started this past year can become reforms in the year ahead,” he said.

Meyer assured the Council that he and his Embassy team would work with the business community to promote the necessary changes, expressing confidence that a more predictable investment climate would benefit businesses in both countries.

He also thanked outgoing Council President Tilak Gunawardana and the leadership board for their contributions, while congratulating the newly elected office bearers as the organisation marked its 10th anniversary.

The Ambassador said he looked forward to working with the Council in the coming year to advance bilateral commercial ties and create conditions in which both Sri Lankan and American businesses could expand.

title: President sets deadlines for key SOE, PPP and Customs laws | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:15
-     - 346

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake - Pic by Lasantha Kumara

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has outlined a February 2027 deadline for presenting key legislation covering State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), public-private partnerships (PPPs), labour reforms and Customs modernisation to Parliament, as the Government seeks to address structural barriers to investment and fiscal sustainability.

Speaking at the inauguration of the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026 on Monday (12), Dissanayake said work on the proposed laws was at different stages of completion, with the SOE legislation expected to reach Cabinet within two weeks.

“Regarding the SOE law, I expect it will be presented to the Cabinet in about two weeks,” he said.

The President said the PPP legislation had already been drafted and submitted to the Legal Draftsman’s Department, with recommendations received. The Government is also consolidating existing labour legislation into a unified framework, while proposed amendments to the Customs Ordinance are being finalised following discussions between the Treasury and the Sri Lanka Customs Department.

“Most likely, all of these bills will be presented to Parliament for approval by February,” he said.

The legislative program forms part of Sri Lanka’s broader structural reform agenda under the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) Extended Fund Facility (EFF), which places emphasis on strengthening public financial management, improving governance and creating a more predictable environment for private investment.

Delays in enacting these reforms have been identified as constraints on the country’s long-term economic competitiveness. Outdated governance arrangements for SOEs can sustain fiscal risks and inefficiencies, while gaps in the legal framework for PPPs can complicate private sector participation in infrastructure and other public projects.

On labour reforms, Dissanayake said around 12 separate labour statutes were currently in force and that the Government was working to consolidate them into a single law.

“A draft bill has already been formulated, though reviewing and finalising it will take some time,” he said, indicating that the process would require further scrutiny before the legislation was ready.

The proposed Customs reforms seek to replace or modernise provisions rooted in the Customs Ordinance of 1869, which the Government considers in need of updating to meet contemporary trade and administrative requirements.

Dissanayake said an agreement had been reached on the proposed amendments after extensive discussions between the Treasury and Customs Department.

“The proposed amendments to the Customs Ordinance are the most appropriate way forward,” he said, adding that the proposals had been submitted to the Legal Draftsman’s Department and that the Government expected the Bill to be finalised promptly.

The reforms are significant for Sri Lanka’s efforts to strengthen revenue mobilisation, improve trade facilitation and attract investment as it continues its post-default economic recovery.

A modernised SOE framework is intended to strengthen accountability and governance across State enterprises, while clearer PPP rules could provide greater certainty for investors considering projects alongside the Government. Labour law consolidation and Customs modernisation are also expected to address regulatory complexity and improve the business environment.

title: Freehold clause, rupee pre-sales and BSI ownership test Port City safeguards | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:14
-     - 274

Parliament’s Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) is seeking the Attorney General’s opinion on whether Colombo Port City apartments can lawfully be sold on a freehold basis when the underlying land is held on 99-year leases. The committee is also pressing for tighter controls over how developers raise presale proceeds and fund construction.

Colombo Port City Economic Commission (CPCEC) Chairman Harsha Amarasekera, PC, told the committee that Section 38 of the Colombo Port City Economic Commission Act, enacted in 2021, empowers the Commission to lease or transfer, on a freehold basis, condominium parcels on land leased to the project company. Because the Commission must join in each conveyance to the end purchaser, he said, the provision was designed to close a gap in the law, and the Commission did not consider it a legal impediment.

Opposition MP Ravi Karunanayake disputed this. He argued that Sri Lanka had told the world the Port City was available only on 99-year leases, so converting this to freehold created a risk for the country, and called for a comprehensive response on the provision’s validity and the country’s obligations. COPF Chairman MP Dr. Harsha de Silva said that if the problem lay in the Act, it was for Parliament, not the Commission, to amend it. A Government member noted that the Attorney General’s Department had vetted the Bill before Parliament approved it.

The funding rules drew equal scrutiny. Amarasekera said the entire construction cost of a primary project must be met in foreign currency raised outside Sri Lanka, and cannot be financed through foreign currency deposits or foreign currency loans from local banks. Apartments, however, may be sold in rupees, even entirely to local buyers. Foreign purchases must be routed through an Inward Investment Account (IIA), a designated account for channelling foreign investment into Sri Lanka. Developers that fail to bring in the full construction cost in foreign currency lose their exemptions under the Act.

Dr. de Silva cited one developer’s public claims that 50% of its units had been sold before the official launch and that its project was valued at $ 300 million. The project is gazetted at $ 152 million, of which Amarasekera said the $ 110 million construction component must come in as foreign currency. He said the Commission would audit actual construction costs rather than rely on disclosed figures.

Dr. de Silva said the regime fell short of global best practice in several respects. Presales face no restriction ahead of construction milestones, developers need not publicly disclose balance sheets, and beneficial ownership is not always clear. He urged the Commission to consider escrow accounts, which hold buyers’ money until set conditions are met, so that presale funds are used for their intended purpose. The Commission said escrow accounts had been discussed and that it was reviewing its condominium management regulations, in consultation with the Legal Draftsman, with a view to adopting such practices in the next revision.

On reporting, the Act requires annual returns, which are due at the end of October under an expanded schedule. Amarasekera said the Commission nonetheless obtains sales and inflow updates from developers almost monthly. Dr. de Silva questioned whether annual reporting was adequate.

The committee’s concerns extended to smaller investors. Its own review of the 68 secondary businesses of strategic importance (BSIs) Gazetted in April found that most listed no parent company and many were incorporated in the British Virgin Islands. Dr. de Silva noted some had invested as little as $ 2,500, yet qualified for BSI status and a 7.5% tax rate. 

Amarasekera could not say what one business Gazetted with a $ 10,000 investment does, but said the Commission examined each application before approval. Where no parent company is listed, the Commission said, the applicant is owned by individuals, who are screened as the beneficial owners. It added that beneficial ownership information is collected at application, and that beneficial ownership provisions from this year’s Companies Act amendments have been made mandatory in annual returns.

Earlier approvals have also faltered. Of 10 approvals the committee reviewed, Dr. de Silva counted five as withdrawn, though the Commission said some of those he named had never been Gazetted. One withdrawn project had promised a seven-star hotel and a vertical art gallery aimed at a Guinness World Record. Its investor had paid only a $ 10,000 application fee and is believed to have forfeited a token deposit to the project company.

Dr. de Silva also urged the Commission to reconsider appointing a full-time legal head. Amarasekera said the Commission relies on the Attorney General for substantive legal advice. Its Director-Commercial, who has a legal background, also covers legal affairs and was recently authorised to sign off as Director-Legal; no Director-Legal salary is being paid. Members also raised an unresolved question over where Port City residents would vote in local government elections, and the Commission said it would seek advice.

title: Port City visa count hits 14,300 as CoPF flags oversight gaps | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:13
-     - 151

The Colombo Port City Economic Commission (CPCEC) has issued 14,300 visas thus far for foreign employees of Port City businesses but cannot vouch for all of them, Parliament’s Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) was told this week. Members questioned whether the regime is being adequately policed amid regional concerns over scam networks and money laundering.

The CPCEC monitors visa holders through monthly reports from businesses and random periodic visits by its officials, Commission Chairman Harsha Amarasekera, PC said. The Commission has a total staff of 16. A committee member noted the visa count averaged about 200 for each business of strategic importance (BSI), and questioned why some firms needed that many given the nature of their operations.

CoPF Chairman MP Dr. Harsha de Silva said the issue went beyond the Commission’s remit, affecting financial sector stability, anti-money laundering compliance and the country’s reputation. Citing official data, he said arrivals in the first quarter of 2026 rose 458% from Myanmar, 258% from Vietnam and 70% from Cambodia, countries widely associated with cyber scam operations. He noted statements issued by the Vietnamese and Chinese embassies, the latter on 29 May 2026, and observed that some foreign newspapers had carried damaging headlines.

The Commission earlier suspended visa recommendations for two APs after five Chinese nationals linked to them were detained and deported. Amarasekera said the suspension lasted three weeks to a month while Commission and immigration officials inspected both businesses. He said that, subject to correction, the five were turned away at the point of entry after failing to satisfactorily explain their purpose. Dr. de Silva observed that, in the absence of specific regulations, deportation orders were being issued for visa violations rather than on scam-related grounds.

Amarasekera said that, to the best of the Commission’s knowledge, no scamming was taking place within the Port City and no regulator had informed it otherwise. Dr. de Silva questioned whether business process outsourcing (BPO) firms, which are required to operate from Grade A office space not yet available within the Port City and currently work from various locations, were adhering to their agreements and not over-employing.

The committee asked the Commission to report within two weeks on how many recently Gazetted BSIs have brought in foreign workers, how many are in the country, their nationalities, length of stay and scope of work. It also asked what share of each firm’s projected foreign hiring had been used.

title: Sri Lanka, EU discuss green energy hub at Trincomalee Port | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:12

Sri Lanka and the European Union (EU) have explored plans to establish a green energy hub at Trincomalee Port, with both sides highlighting the need for a feasibility study to assess the proposal.

The matter was discussed during a meeting between Ports, Civil Aviation and Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka and an EU delegation led by Peteris Ustubs, Director for the Asia-Pacific region, at the Ministry yesterday.

The EU delegation commended the Government’s initiatives in renewable energy generation and energy storage, expressing interest in supporting Sri Lanka’s transition to green energy.

Minister Karunathilaka briefed the delegation on renewable energy projects currently being implemented, while highlighting the need for a feasibility study on the proposed green energy hub at Trincomalee Port.

The discussions also covered plans to develop container terminals to improve the capacity and operational efficiency of the Port of Colombo.

Potential EU assistance for port development projects under the Global Gateway program was also discussed.

Deputy Minister Janitha Ruwan Kodithukku and Ministry Secretary W.W.S. Mangala attended the meeting.

title: Colombo High Court enlarges Jiffry Mohamed on bail in alleged money laundering case | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:05
-     - 113

Colombo High Court Judge Buddhika C. Ragala has enlarged on bail Jiffry Mohamed accused in a money laundering case having considered the submissions made on behalf of the accused and the submissions of the Counsel for the State.

The accused was released on cash bail on 8 October in a sum of Rs 25,000 with two sureties in a sum of Rs. 1 million each. Counsel for the accused Priyantha Nawana PC appearing with Shafi Hussain, Dinali Siva instructed by Asanka Perera submitted that this matter is coming for order following submissions for bail made by senior Counsel M. M. Zuhair PC on the previous date.

Counsel Nawana submitted that Court has the power to grant bail under section 17 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act read with the Bail Act. The accused, it was submitted, has no previous conviction of the commission of any offence whatsoever.

State Counsel Oswald Perera objecting to bail submitted that investigations are ongoing with regard to this accused and enlarging him on bail at this stage could affect the investigations. Court held that indictment has been filed on the basis that investigations into this case have been concluded and made order enlarging the accused on cash bail with two sureties in the High Court case. 

The indictment filed in this case alleges that the accused had committed offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act of ‘unlawful activity’ namely offences including ‘trafficking in drugs’ in violation of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act. Written Submissions filed on behalf of the accused in the connected case in the Negombo Magistrate’s Court has stated that there is no evidence or allegation before Court that the accused had trafficked and/or possessed any quantity of any drug at any time and that he is a trusted businessman maintaining a good record within the business community, handling large volume of advance payments in rupees for importers of goods from overseas exporters and that he himself is not an importer.

Following a further report filed by the Negombo Headquarters Police that there is no new material disclosed against the suspect, the Negombo Magistrate had on 15 September 2026 discharged Jiffry Mohamed from further proceedings in the alleged drug case.

title: Court upholds travel curbs on Hela Clothing Directors | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:05
-     - 307

The Commercial High Court of Colombo has upheld an interim order barring the five Directors of Hela Clothing Ltd., from travelling overseas. The Court rejected their argument that a court exercising civil jurisdiction has no power to restrict a person’s movement, in winding-up proceedings where Commercial Bank of Ceylon PLC accuses them of diverting export proceeds owed to it.

In an order delivered on Tuesday (13), Commercial High Court Judge Chamath Madanayake held that the restriction was justified and within the Court’s powers. He varied it, however, to allow the Directors to travel abroad for predetermined periods with the Court’s prior permission, subject to any conditions it may impose.

The respondent Directors are Panadura Liyanage Dilanka Jinadasa, Albert Rasakantha Rasaiah, Gayan Priyanka Gunawardana, Ranjith Sanath Perera Amaratunga and Aruna De Silva Muthumuni.

The case stems from a resolution passed by Hela Clothing to wind up the company. Commercial Bank then applied under Sections 374, 375 and 376 of the Companies Act No. 7 of 2007, which deal with fraudulent conduct by those running a company and empower the court to inquire into Directors who misapply or retain company money and order them to repay it. The bank is seeking to hold the Directors personally liable for the sums owed to it.

The bank said it had granted Hela Clothing facilities of up to $ 1 million, including pre-shipment loans, which fund an exporter’s costs before goods are shipped. The facilities were to finance export letters of credit and confirmed orders for raw material imports, on the condition that export proceeds were routed through the bank. 

The bank alleged that the Directors fraudulently failed to repay the loans, though they did not dispute the liability, and that they failed to route export proceeds through the bank while concealing the exports.

The bank also alleged that holding company Hela Apparel Holdings PLC had moved to sell some subsidiaries without creditor approval. It further alleged that the Directors had fraudulently appropriated $ 8 million received from Emerald Investments (Private) Ltd, a sum not disclosed in the winding-up petition. 

According to the bank, the company resolved to wind up along with other companies without disclosing its assets and liabilities, the proceeds of exports financed by the bank or the investment. The Court has made no finding on these allegations.

Several other banks have intervened in the case. DFCC Bank has filed a similar application that is yet to be supported, and other banks intend to file applications under similar provisions, the order said. Counsel for HNB and NDB also made submissions.

The Directors have not applied under Section 521 of the Act to revoke the interim orders, but have reserved the right to do so. Their objection was confined to jurisdiction. Their lawyers argued that only a court exercising criminal jurisdiction could impose travel restrictions, that such orders could be made only under the Immigration and Emigration Act, and that neither the Companies Act nor the sections invoked by the bank provided for them. The company also submitted that Sri Lankan courts had never imposed travel restrictions in civil cases, particularly in winding-up matters, and that doing so would open the floodgates.

Judge Madanayake pointed to provisions of the Civil Procedure Code and to Sections 310 and 313 of the Companies Act, which allow the court to order the arrest of Directors who ignore summons and of contributories, those liable to contribute to a company’s assets, who are about to leave the country. 

An arrest order would serve little purpose if the same court could not stop the person leaving, he reasoned. He held that Section 521, which allows the court to make orders ‘as it thinks fit’, and the Court’s inherent powers were wide enough to cover such restrictions.

“In view of the above, I answer the first question against the company and hold that this court has jurisdiction to impose travel restrictions in appropriate circumstances,” the Judge said.

He cited as persuasive authority the English Court of Appeal’s 1986 decision in Bayer AG v Winter, in which a defendant was restrained from leaving the jurisdiction until Mareva and Anton Piller orders, which freeze assets and permit the seizure of evidence, had been executed.

The company had also argued that the bank could not invoke these provisions as no winding-up order had been made and the petition had not even been published. The Judge accepted this in respect of Section 374, which applies only after a winding-up order. He held, however, that Sections 375(2) and 376 operate during the course of a winding up, which under Section 377(2) is deemed to begin when the petition is presented.

The Judge said a creditor, as an outsider with no access to a company’s internal records, cannot be expected to produce all the necessary material. Where the bank alleged that the Directors had not disclosed the company’s exports, the proceeds, its investments, and its assets and liabilities, a greater burden fell on the Directors to reveal information within their exclusive knowledge. 

Their fiduciary duties in such an application extend to the creditor and to the Court, he said, adding that the Court’s role is supervisory rather than that of a mere umpire. The Directors had informed the Court that they would be leaving the country.

The Judge, however, rejected the banks’ contention that travel restrictions should be imposed at the outset of civil proceedings to facilitate possible criminal action, noting that the bank had disclosed in its petition its intention to initiate criminal proceedings and that investigators could obtain such restrictions from a competent court. 

“The powers of this court cannot be extended towards such end,” he said. Any restriction is confined to ensuring the Directors’ presence for examination and the production of books, accounts and information on the company’s affairs, assets, liabilities and investments, he added.

The travel restriction was among interim orders issued on 25 September, 2026, when President’s Counsel Shivan Coorey supported Commercial Bank’s applications against Hela Clothing and Foundation Garments (Private) Ltd. He told the Court that the two companies and Hela Apparel Holdings shared common Directors and a registered address. The Court issued notice on the first to fifth respondent Directors in both cases and granted interim orders under prayers (f) to (i) in the Hela Clothing case and (g) to (i) in the Foundation Garments case, subject to the bank depositing Rs. 1 million as security. It also issued the travel restriction under prayer (j) and directed that the interim orders be communicated to the Registrar of Companies by email.

Coorey told the Court that the bank had extended a $ 3 million pre-shipment facility to Foundation Garments on the same conditions, that each company had guaranteed the other’s debts, and that Hela Apparel Holdings had given letters of comfort undertaking that the companies would not be liquidated. 

He said the bank issued a demand on 27 July, 2026, which Jinadasa acknowledged on 10 August, 2026, informing the bank of the planned winding-up applications. Coorey argued that exporters are required by law to repatriate export proceeds, citing a Gazette dated 1 July, 2024, and told the Court the case reflected a pattern of exporters taking assets out of the country using public money.

title: Customs surpasses Rs. 2.2 t annual revenue target | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 06:02
-     - 86

Sri Lanka Customs has surpassed its original 2026 revenue target of Rs. 2,207 billion, collecting Rs. 2,208 billion by 13 October, nearly a month ahead of the date it achieved the previous year’s target.

The achievement marks the second consecutive year Customs has exceeded its annual revenue target ahead of schedule, despite setting a lower initial target for 2026 amid expectations of a significant decline in vehicle imports early in the year.

In 2025, Customs reached its original revenue target of Rs. 2,115 billion on 11 November before exceeding a revised target of Rs. 2,241 billion to collect Rs. 2,557.5 billion by year-end. This represented a record collection and a 64.6% increase over the Rs. 1,553 billion recorded in 2024.

The original revenue target for 2026 was 13.5% below the previous year’s target, reflecting anticipated revenue pressures from vehicle imports. However, collections have already exceeded the target, raising the prospect of another revision if the pace of revenue generation continues.

The department is accelerating digitalisation of its operations. Digital signatures for customs declarations were introduced on 1 October, with the submission process scheduled to become fully digital from 19 October. Declarations submitted under the previous paper-based method will no longer be accepted thereafter.

It reflects the strength, professionalism and expertise of the Delmege Insurance Brokers team, and, most importantly, the trust placed in us by our clients and business partners. We are extremely proud of the team and remain committed to supporting their continued growth and pursuit of excellence.”

Delmege Insurance Brokers CEO Sidantha Karunaratne attributed the achievement to the company’s people, clients and long-standing industry partnerships.

“Being ranked No. 1 for three consecutive years demonstrates consistency and the confidence our clients and partners place in us. This achievement belongs to our team, whose expertise and commitment are evident every day. Our focus now is to build on this success by strengthening our capabilities, enhancing our service and creating lasting value for every client we serve,” he added.

The company’s professional standing has also been reflected in industry recognition. The confidence of Delmege’s clients is equally reflected in their experience. Echoing this sentiment, GP Garments Ltd., Chief Finance and Compliance Officer Patrice Jermann said: “For more than a decade, we have relied on Delmege for professional guidance, responsive service and timely support whenever challenges arise. Congratulations to the entire Delmege team.”

For Delmege Insurance Brokers, retaining the No. 1 position for three successive years is both a milestone and a responsibility—to continue raising standards, strengthening relationships and delivering the expertise and service that have earned the confidence of the 

market.

title: Digital Summit Asia 2026 seeks to position Sri Lanka as Asia’s digital epicentre | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 04:26
-     - 26

From right: DMASL Executive Committee Member and Commercial Bank of Ceylon MarTech and Digital Strategy Lead Shanaka Rathnayake (Moderator), eTranzact Ghana CEO and Board Member Dr. John Obeng Apea, Visa CMO and Head of Marketing – India and South Asia Gaurav Ramdev, PayMedia Founder/CEO Kanishka Weeramunda, HNB Chief Innovation Officer Chandima Cooray, and Equity Group Holdings Group Director – International Trade Relations and CWEIC Hub Director – East and Central Africa A.Q. Hamza

By Safna Malik

A strong global digital presence can help Sri Lankan businesses enter overseas markets and lift foreign-exchange earnings, Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne said. Addressing Digital Summit Asia Sri Lanka 2026, organised by the Digital Marketers Association of Sri Lanka (DMASL), in Colombo, he said the Government would focus on five key areas, including digitalising public services and traditional sectors, developing digital skills, promoting cashless payments, expanding the digital industry and achieving $ 5 billion in digital exports by 2030 as part of Sri Lanka’s digital transformation plan.

Accessing or developing technology is not the greatest challenge; Sri Lanka has the resources and talent to do so. “The difficult part is changing human behaviour,” he said. Although QR and digital-payment options are widely available, many consumers continue to withdraw cash before making purchases.

Taking LankaQR as an example, Weeraratne said that, despite being available for more than five years, QR-based payments have yet to achieve widespread adoption. The Government’s objective is to make LankaQR the first choice for consumers and merchants alike.

Changing this will require a major shift in transaction habits, with digital payments becoming the first choice over cash. Effective marketing is needed to communicate the convenience and advantages of digital payments.

In today’s connected world, he said, geography matters less than a country’s capabilities, creativity and the trust it earns for the work it delivers. Meanwhile, entrepreneurs are launching new businesses, supported by a broader community seeking to position Sri Lanka as Asia’s Epicentre for digital marketing, creativity, technology, innovation and business.

MullenLowe MENA Executive Creative Director Prerna Mehra opened the learning sessions with her keynote, “You’re in a toxAic relationship,” setting the tone for a presentation that placed AI in a human context.

She said people often treat AI like a vending machine: insert a prompt, press a button and expect brilliance. But when results disappoint, the response is often simply: “I don’t like it,” “make it better,” “make it human,” or “try again.”

AI does not require politeness or validation; it requires clarity. Mehra outlined common red flags in this relationship: vague briefs, missing context, changing instructions, feedback that dismisses output without proper guidance, and letting AI decide which option is best when that decision and responsibility must remain human.

Without this clarity, AI can accelerate creative work but risk producing “AI slop”: generic, repetitive and emotionally empty content that can reduce brand quality and push audiences away.

To counter this, give AI clear direction, relevant background, brand language and success criteria, specific feedback, updated briefs when needed, and human judgement. She said AI should be treated as a tool for developing ideas, not as a replacement for thinking.

In a session titled “From local to global: Expanding your local business worldwide,” Yell Worldwide Founder and Chief Executive Ohm Dissara Udomdej said the digital economy has made international expansion more accessible for regional businesses.

Cultural context, he said, is a form of currency: understanding how people think, what they value and what feels familiar determines whether a brand can earn relevance in a new market. AI can translate words, but not culture; effective communication still depends on human judgement, tone, humour and local references.

For Sri Lanka, he said the country’s unique culture offers a strong base for global expansion. Every market has its own “creative dialect,” and even regional differences within one country matter. Brands must align with local culture rather than impose foreign ideas.

Businesses should define their brand, purpose and values, then adapt their storytelling for international audiences while protecting their identity and respecting local cultures. AI should remain a supporting tool, he added; with the right partners and cultural understanding, local businesses can connect with the world.

In the session “From watch it to want it: The TikTok effect,’’ TikTok (ByteDance) Client Partner, CSAA: Consumer Business, Farah Mehdi, outlined how TikTok has evolved from an entertainment platform into a demand-generation engine that moves users from watching to wanting to buying. 

With over two billion monthly users globally and 8.6 million in Sri Lanka, where TikTok logs 38 billion views and 37 million video creations monthly, the platform offers unmatched reach and participation. 63% of users are comfortable seeing creators in brand campaigns, and such exposure significantly lifts product research and purchase intent. Mehdi advised businesses to run consistent campaigns that reach at least half the target audience, deliver two or more exposures per week over four weeks, and measure outcomes, positioning TikTok not just as an awareness channel but as a lever for demand creation and sales growth.

Under the session, “Making people care: What your brain does before you decide,’’ Casual Director of Narrative Strategy, Oliver Atkinson, argued that most advertising fails because it never gets registered in the brain. Ads pass through like radio signals on an untuned channel. In an age of endless AI content, the scarcity is no longer creativity. It is connection and care.

Atkinson explained that about 95% of decisions happen below conscious awareness. The rational mind acts as a press office, giving reasons for decisions the subconscious has already made.

Speaking about brain behaviour, he said resonance gets past the brain’s filter when a message feels relatable. Immersion keeps attention long enough to drive action. Creating interest is necessary, but action is the goal. The aim is to make people buy, remember, or change.

In this AI world, the advantage will not go to whoever produces the most content. It will go to whoever makes people feel connected, and the question remains whether we should produce content or should be designing connections.

mktgstack co-founders Varun Khiatani and Namrata Chawla, during their session Stop Answering Briefs, Start Answering Consumers, said brands and agencies must understand the real consumer and business problem before building a solution.

Khiatani said marketers need to get closer to people instead of relying only on screens, reports and trends. “If you remain a laptop creator, you will not only become less creative; you will also become less informed,” he said, warning that briefs can otherwise reflect a company’s message rather than consumer needs.

Briefs often prescribe solutions before defining the problem, Chawla said. “Why do we put the solution inside the brief before we have properly examined the question?” She added that ROI cannot be a universal metric, because each marketing activity should be judged by the business problem and behaviour it aims to change.

Chawla stressed that a campaign idea alone is not enough. “If the idea is strong but nobody sees it, it may not solve the business problem.” Khiatani added that shareable content can turn attention into distribution: “Create a strong idea. Use social content to generate attention. Build an audience around the product.” Their key takeaway from the session was, “We do not answer briefs. We answer the right questions, and we answer consumers.”

Moderated by DMASL Executive Committee Member and Commercial Bank of Ceylon PLC Martech and Digital Strategy Lead Shanaka Rathnayaka, the panel discussion, Payments Are Getting Smarter: What Does That Mean For The Customer Relationship, brought together PayMedia Ltd. Founder and CEO Kanishka Weeramunda, eTranzact Ghana Ltd. CEO and Board Member Dr. John Obeng Apea, Visa CMO and Head of Marketing, India and South Asia Gaurav Ramdev, HNB Chief Innovation Officer Chandima Cooray, and Equity Group Holdings Group Director for International Trade Relations and Commonwealth Enterprise and Investment Council (CWEIC) Hub Director for East and Central Africa AQ Hamza to explore how technology is reshaping trust, choice and accountability in financial services.

Invisible payments, visible choice

Weeramunda said payments are becoming more embedded and less visible, but customers must still consciously choose the brands they trust. He argued that businesses cannot leave these decisions entirely to automation. “The opportunity lies in making our brand the one customer deliberately choose, rather than leaving the decision to an automated system,” he said.

Automation needs accountability

Apea argued that the real test of a digital financial relationship begins when an algorithm rejects a customer or a payment is declined. While automation can expand access to credit and services, institutions must explain negative decisions, offer alternatives and treat customers fairly. Without clear communication, he warned, people may lose confidence in digital systems and return to cash.

He added that this is particularly important for small businesses, which often lack the resources to manage complex payment systems. “Trust and confidence are essential,” Apea said, stressing that providers must explain decisions and support merchants after problems arise.

Removing merchant friction

Cooray noted that many small merchants still depend on manual CEFT transfers, requiring customers to enter account details, select the right bank and complete several error-prone steps. He argued that digital banking should remove such friction by allowing businesses to accept card payments directly through a mobile app.

Using the HNB Mobile App and its HNB Accept capability as an example, Cooray said mobile-led payment acceptance can remove the need for separate POS hardware, reduce input errors, speed up transactions and give merchants more control over payments.

Payments are part of a journey

Ramdev said payments are no longer a standalone interaction but part of a wider customer journey across online and offline channels. He illustrated this with an AI assistant that could guide a customer from recipe recommendations to ingredient purchases, checkout, delivery and cooking instructions.

“In that type of experience, the payment is only one part of the journey,” Ramdev said. He argued that brands must remain useful and relevant throughout the experience, rather than appearing only at the point of transaction.

When payments fail

Pointing payment failures as a crucial moment related to customer relationships. Ramdev said providers must take responsibility, clearly explain errors and communicate transparently about a customer’s money. “A payment failure is not only a technical incident. It is also a brand moment,” he said.

Apea agreed that speed without explanation is not enough. Customers need to know what happened, who is accountable and when the issue will be resolved. He argued that properly managed failures can build loyalty, while poor communication can quickly weaken trust.

The human layer matters

Apea emphasised that digital systems can deliver speed and scale but cannot fully replace empathy and judgement. “Particularly in financial services, a customer may need more than an automated message,” he said.

He called for a hybrid model in which algorithms enable faster decisions while human support provides fairness, inclusion and accountability, especially when customers are rejected, confused or lack confidence in digital services.

Sri Lanka’s cross-border opportunity

Hamza said emerging-market digital ecosystems must look beyond their regions to grow. South Asian technology and digital frameworks, he argued, could serve markets in East Africa and across Commonwealth networks.

He urged Sri Lankan agencies and tech firms to develop solutions for shared emerging-market needs, including fintech, localised e-commerce and data-driven consumer insights. The challenge, he noted, is less about technical ability than navigating compliance, payment gateways and local regulations.

Trade organisations can help home-grown firms access institutional buyers and corporate networks, he added. Drawing on Equity Group’s experience in Africa, Hamza called for smoother cross-border trade channels to help regional talent and technology services scale.

The panel’s collective message was that smarter payments must remain inclusive, reliable and human-centred. Trust will depend on how well brands support customers through moments of choice, help and crisis and whether people feel understood and included throughout the journey.

The first day also featured breakout sessions led by international speakers, including Senator We Run Ads Founder Ovais Ahamed on, “The thinking performance marketer: The way to be relevant in the AI age.” Swiggy AVP Marketing and Creative Head Prateek on, “Why so serious? Humour in advertising communication.” Voxy Media Southeast Asia Business Head Naved Qureshi on the topic, “From creator activity to creator infrastructure: Why brands need an operating system, not another influencer campaign.”

The summit continued into its second day, with Ramdev returning to deliver the opening keynote, “Before brands, there was trust,” extending the discussion on customer relationships and trust.

DMASL vice-presidents and summit co-chairs Gayathri Seneviratne and Shalendra Mendis described Digital Summit Asia Sri Lanka 2026 as an industry milestone and regional opportunity. Formerly known as Digital Summit Sri Lanka, the summit was renamed to position Sri Lanka as the Epicentre of Asia’s digital marketing, creative and innovation industries.

Powered by Visa, the two-day summit featured thought leadership, interactive and breakout sessions, and a first-of-its-kind Night Summit. Its full-day agenda connected Sri Lankan professionals with international and regional expertise while creating greater visibility and opportunities for local talent. Businesses also had the opportunity to engage with speakers, partners and delegates, exchange ideas, build relationships and take practical insights back to their organisations.

They said Sri Lanka’s digital industry must unite to compete globally. “When an industry comes together like this, we have an opportunity together as a community. We can take on anyone in the world if we align in the right ways.” For brands and agencies, global growth will depend on collaboration, shared learning and a stronger collective presence beyond Sri Lanka.

Litro Gas Lanka Ltd., will buy its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) for 2027 from OQ Trading Ltd., at the Saudi Aramco Contract Price plus $ 133.93 per metric tonne, Cabinet Spokesperson Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said on Tuesday. The Saudi Aramco Contract Price is the monthly benchmark price for LPG.

He was speaking at the media briefing on decisions taken at Monday’s (12) Cabinet meeting. Dr. Jayatissa said the contract covers 420,000 metric tonnes, plus or minus 20%, with a guaranteed minimum of 336,000 metric tonnes. It runs for 12 months from 1 January, 2027.

The previous supplier was Geogas Trading SA of Switzerland which supplied LPG from the US.

Founder and MD Marlon Ferreira and Inventor of the PACCP-X Framework

Entrepreneur Denham Marlon Ferreira has secured UK trademark registration for the PACCP-X figurative mark through the UK Intellectual Property Office (UK IPO). Registration No. UK00004413460 is held personally by Exterminators PLC Founder and MD Marlon Ferreira and covers pest control and termite control services. 

Guided by “Prevent. Predict. Protect”, PACCP-X helps pest management teams assess risk, identify root causes, choose suitable controls and strengthen prevention. Its seven areas are; pest intelligence, analysis of root causes, critical containment, control optimisation, preventive control points, predictive analytics, and continuous learning and improvement.

In Sri Lanka, PACCP-X is applied through PESTMAC 3G in the food industry, combining targeted treatments, monitoring, risk assessment and digital reporting. It also supports HotelGuard 360™ in the hotel and hospitality sector, addressing pest risks across guest spaces, food environments, property, water and biosecurity. 

Sentario UK Ltd., in technical collaboration with Exterminators PLC, has launched PACCP-X Maldives Resorts. The program offers resorts pest-risk reporting, staff training, digital monitoring, specialist support and a Resort Readiness Review. The companies plan to work directly with resorts, providing consultation and implementation support. PACCP-X training programs and workshops have been delivered at organisations in Sri Lanka. Participants who pass the assessment receive PACCP-X Level 1 certificates.

Ferreira is inviting pest management companies in eligible markets outside Sri Lanka, the Maldives and the UK to explore training and licensing opportunities. Subject to local brand clearance and agreed terms, these may include team training, assessment, implementation resources and written authorisation to use approved framework materials. 

“Effective pest management begins with understanding risk, addressing its causes and strengthening prevention over time. PACCP-X gives teams a practical way to apply that approach,” said Ferreira. 

During October 2026, the company will provide free, point-based pest risk assessment reports for food businesses and hotels, prepared in accordance with the PACCP-X framework.

title: Saudi Supreme Court sets aside death sentence on Sri Lankan Anojan Sivarasa | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 15 October 2026 05:57
-     - 32

Anojan Sivarasa

The Supreme Court of Saudi Arabia has set aside the death sentence imposed on Sri Lankan national Anojan Sivarasa, marking a significant breakthrough in the country’s diplomatic and legal efforts to secure a favourable outcome in his case.

Foreign Affairs and Foreign Employment Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra announced the development yesterday (14), describing it as “a major relief for Anojan Sivarasa” following continued efforts by the Government of Sri Lanka.

The Foreign Affairs Ministry of also confirmed the decision in a statement, saying it brings immense relief to Sivarasa and his family.

The Government expressed its appreciation to the Government of Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism, the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment, and the Sri Lankan and Saudi legal teams for their dedicated efforts.

As part of these efforts, a Sri Lankan delegation comprising legal experts travelled to Saudi Arabia to engage with the relevant authorities on the case and explore avenues for challenging the death sentence.

The delegation included Member of Parliament Mohamed Faiszer Musthapha, PC; Consul General of Sri Lanka in Jeddah M.T. Mohamed Laffar; Attorney General’s Department Additional Solicitor General Hafeez Azard Navavi, PC; K. A. Upul Indika Kumarapperuma PC, Attorney-at-Law Farisz Fazal Abdul Hafeel Mohomed and Coordinating Secretary to MP Musthapha Mohamed Riyasdeen Silmy.

During the visit, the delegation met Saudi legal representatives to discuss the case and determine the appropriate procedures for filing an appeal before the Saudi Supreme Court.

Musthapha said discussions were held with local lawyers to ensure the appeal was prepared and submitted in accordance with Saudi Arabian law.

Sivarasa had been sentenced to death by a Saudi appellate court in a case reportedly linked to allegations of blasphemy arising from a comment he posted on Facebook.

Mass Media Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa had also previously stated that diplomatic efforts were underway to seek a reduction in the sentence.
